title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 181
paragraphs: Those have now been mentioned who are nomad Libyans living along the coast; and above these, inland, is the part of Libya that has wild beasts, and above the wild-beast region stretches a raised belt of sand extending from Egyptian Thebes to the Pillars of Heracles. In this belt, at intervals of about ten days' journey, there are great lumps of salt forming hills, and from the middle of the salt on top of each hill there rises up a spring of cold, sweet water; and around the spring people live, at the furthest limit toward the desert, above the wild-beast region. First, at ten days' journey from Thebes, are the Ammonians, whose temple is derived from that of Theban Zeus—for the image of Zeus in Thebes too, as I have said before, has the head of a ram. They happen also to have another water from a spring, which in the early morning is warm; when the market fills, cooler; at noon it is quite cold, and then they water their gardens with it; but as the day declines it abates from its coldness, until, when the sun sets, the water is warm; and it continues to grow still hotter until midnight, when it boils and throws up bubbles; after midnight passes, it gradually cools again until daybreak. This spring is called the Fountain of the Sun.
